runs.question: Under section 201(a), who initially owns copyright in a joint work?

claims.text: Under section 201(a), the initial owners of copyright in a joint work are the coauthors of the work.

evidence.quote: (a) INITIAL OWNERSHIP.—Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work.

claims.text: The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work.

evidence.quote: The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work.

runs.question: Under section 201(a), who initially owns copyright in a joint work, and under section 204(a), what does a voluntary transfer of copyright ownership require?

claims.text: Under section 201(a), the initial owners of copyright in a work are the authors of the work, and in the case of a joint work, the coauthors are coowners of the copyright.

evidence.quote: (a) INITIAL OWNERSHIP.—Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work.
The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work.

claims.text: Under section 204(a), a voluntary transfer of copyright ownership requires that the transfer be in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or by such owner’s duly authorized agent.

evidence.quote: (a) A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner’s duly authorized agent.

claims.text: The requirement under section 204(a) applies to transfers other than those by operation of law.

evidence.quote: (a) A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner’s duly authorized agent.

claims.text: A note or memorandum of the transfer may serve as valid evidence if it is in writing and signed by the owner or their duly authorized agent.

evidence.quote: Under subsection (a), a transfer of copyright ownership (other than one brought about by operation of law) is valid only if there exists an instrument of conveyance, or alternatively a ‘‘note or memorandum of the transfer,’’ which is in writing and signed by the copyright owner ‘‘or such owner’s duly authorized agent.’’ Subsection (b) makes clear that a notarial or consular acknowledgment is not essential to the validity of any transfer, whether executed in the United States or abroad.
